records.title: Perf regression: trtllm_allreduce_fusion one-shot Lamport ~2µs/call slower since 0.6.8 (TP=2 bf16, Blackwell)
records.body:
## Summary

The fused AllReduce+RMSNorm **one-shot Lamport** kernel reached via
`flashinfer.comm.trtllm_allreduce_fusion(..., use_oneshot=True)`
(`tensorrt_llm::_v1::kernels::ar_fusion::allreduce_fusion_kernel_oneshot_lamport`)
has a **~2 µs higher fixed per-call latency in 0.6.12 (and 0.6.8) than in 0.6.6**
on Blackwell, TP=2, bf16. The overhead is a fixed cost, so it hurts most in the
small/medium token regime (≤256 tokens, ~+14%) and is hidden for large,
compute-bound token counts.

In a real workload (Llama-3.1-8B, TP=2 prefill) this kernel dominates GPU time and
the per-call overhead accumulates into a measurable first-token-time regression.

## Environment

- GPU: 2× NVIDIA B300 (sm_103a), NVLink P2P (NVLS disabled)
- dtype bf16, hidden_dim 4096, TP=2
- Compared: flashinfer-python **0.6.6** vs **0.6.12** (regression first appears at **0.6.8**)
- The reproducer depends only on `flashinfer.comm` + `torch.distributed` (no TensorRT-LLM).

## Reproducer

```bash
torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 flashinfer_ar_fusion_repro.py
# run once per flashinfer version; compare rank-0 median_us
```

```python
import os, torch, torch.distributed as dist
import flashinfer.comm as fc
from flashinfer.comm.trtllm_ar import AllReduceFusionPattern

HIDDEN, MAX_TOKEN, DTYPE, RMS_EPS = 4096, 2048, torch.bfloat16, 1e-5
WARMUP, ITERS = 30, 100
TOKENS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]

def main():
    dist.init_process_group("nccl")
    rank, world = dist.get_rank(), dist.get_world_size()
    torch.cuda.set_device(rank); dev = torch.device(f"cuda:{rank}"); pg = dist.group.WORLD
    ws = fc.trtllm_create_ipc_workspace_for_all_reduce_fusion(rank, world, MAX_TOKEN, HIDDEN, group=pg)
    workspace_ptrs = ws[1]
    gamma = torch.randn(HIDDEN, dtype=DTYPE, device=dev)
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"{torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)} TP={world} hidden={HIDDEN} {DTYPE}")
        print(f"{'tokens':>8} {'median_us':>11} {'p90_us':>9}")
    for n in TOKENS:
        ar_in = torch.randn(n, HIDDEN, dtype=DTYPE, device=dev)
        residual = torch.randn(n, HIDDEN, dtype=DTYPE, device=dev)
        norm_out, res_out = torch.empty_like(ar_in), torch.empty_like(residual)
        def call():
            fc.trtllm_allreduce_fusion(
                allreduce_in=ar_in, world_size=world, world_rank=rank, token_num=n,
                hidden_dim=HIDDEN, workspace_ptrs=workspace_ptrs, launch_with_pdl=False,
                use_oneshot=True, trigger_completion_at_end=False, fp32_acc=False,
                pattern_code=AllReduceFusionPattern.kARResidualRMSNorm, allreduce_out=None,
                residual_in=residual, residual_out=res_out, norm_out=norm_out, quant_out=None,
                scale_out=None, rms_gamma=gamma, rms_eps=RMS_EPS, scale_factor=None, layout_code=None)
        for _ in range(WARMUP): call()
        torch.cuda.synchronize(); dist.barrier(group=pg)
        evs = [(torch.cuda.Event(True), torch.cuda.Event(True)) for _ in range(ITERS)]
        for s, e in evs: s.record(); call(); e.record()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        ts = sorted(s.elapsed_time(e)*1e3 for s, e in evs)
        if rank == 0: print(f"{n:>8} {ts[len(ts)//2]:>11.2f} {ts[int(len(ts)*0.9)]:>9.2f}")
        dist.barrier(group=pg)
    dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Results (median per-call latency, µs)

| tokens | 0.6.6 | 0.6.12 | Δ |
|-------:|------:|-------:|----:|
| 1      | 16.6  | 18.7   | +2.1 |
| 2      | 15.4  | 17.7   | +2.3 |
| 4      | 15.6  | 17.7   | +2.1 |
| 8      | 15.5  | 17.6   | +2.1 |
| 16     | 15.6  | 17.6   | +2.0 |
| 32     | 15.6  | 17.7   | +2.1 |
| 64     | 15.6  | 17.7   | +2.1 |
| 128    | 15.6  | 17.7   | +2.1 |
| 256    | 17.5  | 17.7   | +0.2 |
| 512    | 21.8  | 22.2   | +0.4 |
| 1024   | 33.0  | 33.1   | ~0   |
| 2048   | 62.0  | 62.6   | +0.6 |

The gap is a near-constant **~2 µs/call** added in 0.6.12, dominant at ≤256 tokens
(~+14% at the small end), negligible once the kernel becomes compute-bound.

## Ask

- What changed in the one-shot Lamport `trtllm_allreduce_fusion` path between 0.6.6
  and 0.6.8 that added this fixed per-call overhead (launch config, extra sync,
  buffer init, host-side prep)?
- Can the small-token path be restored to the 0.6.6 latency?

records.title: [SM120] Sparse-MLA DSV4 decode+prefill kernels not instantiated for topk=256
records.body:
## Summary

The SM120 sparse-MLA **DSV4** kernels are only instantiated for `topk ∈ {128, 512, 1024, 2048}`. An attention call with **`topk=256`** has no kernel in either the decode or the prefill path and fails:

**decode** (`num_tokens ≤ 64`) — `_paged_attention` in `flashinfer/mla/_sparse_mla_sm120.py` finds `(num_heads, topk)` absent from `_DECODE_DSV4_DISPATCH`, so it falls through to the prefill orchestrator (`csrc/sparse_mla_sm120.cu`), which is decode-rejecting:
```
Check failed: num_tokens > 64 (7 vs. 64) : Decode (num_tokens <= 64) must go through
sparse_mla_sm120_decode_dsv3_2 or sparse_mla_sm120_decode_dsv4; got num_tokens=7
```

**prefill** (`num_tokens > 64`) — `sparse_mla_prefill_dispatch` → `dispatch_dsv4_single` in `csrc/sparse_mla_sm120_prefill.cu` has no `topk == 256` branch and returns false:
```
Unsupported sparse-MLA prefill configuration: model=DSV4 num_heads=32 topk=256
page_block_size=64 topk_extra=0 extra_page_block_size=0
```

`topk=256` is a valid shape (`256 = 4 × BI(64)`, between the instantiated 128 and 512); it's simply missing from the instantiation grids.

## Repro / context

Serving DeepSeek-V4 + DSpark speculative decoding on vLLM, SM120 (RTX PRO 6000, TP=2). The DSpark draft's sliding-window (`swa_only`) layers issue sparse-MLA attention with `num_heads=32` (64 heads / TP2), `topk=256`, `page_block_size=64`, `d_qk=512`, `extra_topk=0`. Warmup hits the decode path (`num_tokens ≤ 64`) → the fallthrough assert; the flashinfer autotune dummy run hits the prefill path (`num_tokens > 64`) → the unsupported-config error.

## Fix

Adding the `topk=256` instantiations resolves it end-to-end (verified serving):

- `csrc/sparse_mla_sm120_decode_dsv4.cu` — `DSV4_DISPATCH(H, 256)` for `H ∈ {8,16,32,64,128}`
- `flashinfer/mla/_sparse_mla_sm120.py` — the `(H, 256)` pairs in `_DECODE_DSV4_DISPATCH`
- `csrc/sparse_mla_sm120_prefill.cu` (`dispatch_dsv4_single`) — `else if (topk == 256) DISPATCH_BY_NH_CM(FP8, 256);` (FP8 per the existing perf-mode comment; smem-safe since FP8-512 already builds)

Tested against main @ `b5ac097e`.

records.title: [Bug] SM120 XQA MLA fp8: rowMaxLog2e metadata intermittently corrupted in the producer-to-consumer X handoff (masked today; blocks return_lse #3653)
records.body:
### Summary

On SM120 (RTX PRO 6000, CUDA 13), the fp8 XQA MLA decode kernel (`csrc/xqa/mla_sm120.cu`) intermittently delivers a corrupted `rowMaxLog2e` to the consumer CTAs, while the X payload and `rowSum` in the same `CgaXBuffer` transfer arrive intact. Nobody sees this today because nothing consumes the transferred row max in the shipping configuration: the single-block output normalization is invariant to the row max (numerator and denominator share the same `exp2(-M)`), and the only real consumers - the multi-block merge (`mergePartialOutputs`) and an LSE output - are respectively disabled (`launchMLAFlashInfer`: "MLA disables multi-block mode for now") and not implemented yet. It does mean the affected rows silently lose some precision, and it blocks both #3653 (`return_lse`) and any future multi-block re-enable, since the merge trusts the per-chunk `rowMaxLog2e`/`rowSum` pairs.

### How I found it

Implementing `return_lse` for #3653 (`lse = rowMaxLog2e + log2(rowSum)`, written from the consumer epilogue) made the corruption visible as huge finite LSE outliers. Against the fa2 MLA wrapper and a pure-torch logsumexp (which agree with each other to 4 decimals), the XQA LSE for single elements comes back at +26 to +213 in log2 units where the true value is ~9-10, on 1-4 elements out of ~100k per affected run, 1-4 affected cases per 396-case run of the existing fp8/bf16 test grids. Run-to-run on identical inputs: 10 of 39 repeat trials produced at least one differing LSE element (fa2 reference: 0 drift).

### Repro

Branch with the LSE detector: https://github.com/waynehacking8/flashinfer/tree/wayne/xqa-mla-return-lse (adds `return_lse` to `xqa_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla`).

Poison harness: fill the workspace scratch region with `0x7e` bytes before every call, so any read of not-yet-written scratch is loud. On the LSE branch (no other kernel changes), batch=64, page=128, seq lens randint(1,1024), fp8:

```python
ws = torch.zeros(128 * 1024 * 1024, dtype=torch.int8, device="cuda")
for t in range(600):
    ws[8 * 1024 * 1024:].fill_(0x7E)  # poison scratch (cgaXBuf area)
    _ = torch.randn(2048, 2048, device="cuda") @ torch.randn(2048, 2048, device="cuda")
    out, lse = flashinfer.decode.xqa_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(
        query=query, kv_cache=kv_cache.unsqueeze(1), workspace_buffer=ws,
        qk_nope_head_dim=128, kv_lora_rank=512, qk_rope_head_dim=64,
        block_tables=block_tables, seq_lens=seq_lens_tensor, max_seq_len=max_seq_len,
        bmm1_scale=sm_scale, bmm2_scale=1.0, return_lse=True)
    assert lse.max().item() < 30  # true LSE is ~<=15 for these inputs
```

Measured rates (300-600 poisoned trials each, RTX PRO 6000, CUDA 13, main @ c53229ef + LSE patch):

| configuration | corruption events |
|---|---|
| fp8, LSE = rowMax + log2(rowSum) | 6/600, worst LSE 233.9 |
| fp8, LSE = rowMax only (debug) | 5/300, worst raw rowMax 165.7 |
| fp8, LSE = log2(rowSum) only (debug) | 0/300 |
| bf16, LSE = rowMax + log2(rowSum) | 0/300 |

So the corrupted datum is `rowMaxLog2e` specifically (the tail 512 B of the 9 KB `CgaXBuffer`), `rowSum` (the adjacent 512 B) stayed clean, and the bf16 kernel is clean under the identical harness. `enable_pdl` on/off are both affected. Everything is timing dependent: the same test passes in isolation and fails 1-4 cases when the full grid runs back-to-back.

### What I ruled out (each measured with the poison harness, 300-600 trials)

- `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` before the `sendX` TMA store (the tma_store_fence pattern): no change.
- `fence.proxy.async.global` on both sides of the global `cgaXBuf` handoff: no change.
- `griddepcontrol.wait` at kernel entry: no change for this bug. (Separately: the kernel is launched with the PDL attribute but never calls `acqBulk()`, unlike `mha.cu`/`mha_sm90.cu` - that still looks worth fixing on its own.)
- 20 us delay between the consumer's produced-wait and its TMA load: no change, so it is not a simple store-completion latency race.

### Pointers

- The consumer-side handoff carries the original author's own doubt (`Consumer::loadX`): `// @fixme: check if this works. If it doesn't, randomly pick some data from dstX and dstRowSum and use STAS + arrive_tx to avoid fence.`
- The corrupted values look like plausible arithmetic results in the wrong scale regime (tens to low hundreds), not raw bit garbage, and in one poisoned run an event landed within 0.4 of `log2(poison_float)` - I could not reduce these observations to a single mechanism.

The LSE feature itself is ready on the branch above (fa2/torch-verified; the bf16 grid is 100% stable across repeated runs). I can send it either as a bf16-only PR now (fp8 + return_lse raising until this is fixed), or as the full PR once the metadata path is reliable - whichever you prefer. Happy to test candidate fixes on this card; it reproduces within a minute here.

### Environment

RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q Workstation Edition (SM120), CUDA 13.0, driver 580.159.03, flashinfer main @ c53229ef, torch 2.11.0+cu130.

records.title: fix(gemm): handle linear MXFP8 scales in bmm_mxfp8 cuDNN
records.body:
My PR to fix a bug w/ swizzling for MXFP8 tensors fell through the cracks and never got reviewed.

Previously, bmm_mxfp8 always built the cuDNN MXFP8 graph with scale tensors declared as F8_128x4. That was correct for swizzled scales, but incorrect when the inputs were quantized with is_sf_swizzled_layout=False, which produces linear scales.

This PR adds an explicit sf_layout argument to bmm_mxfp8

records.title: BF16 TinyGEMM can hang on Blackwell SM103 for large projection shapes
records.body:
## Summary

On Blackwell B300A / SM103, BF16 `mm_bf16` can hang indefinitely for some large projection shapes when TinyGEMM is used. This is visible both when calling `backend="tinygemm"` directly and when `backend="auto"` / vLLM's FlashInfer BF16 path autotunes across candidates that include `tinygemm2`.

The hang looks like a CUDA kernel that never completes: GPU utilization stays high and the Python process blocks in `torch.cuda.synchronize()` / the FlashInfer autotuner profiling synchronize. The CUDA context cannot be recovered in-process; the benchmark watchdog had to kill and restart the worker.

## Environment

- GPU: B300A / Blackwell, `torch.cuda.get_device_capability() == (10, 3)`
- Device name from PyTorch: `NVIDIA Graphics Device`
- FlashInfer: `0.6.12`
- PyTorch: `2.11.0+cu130`
- CUDA: `13.0`
- Python: `3.12.3`

## Minimal repro

This repro runs each case in a subprocess because a hung TinyGEMM launch leaves the CUDA context wedged.

```python
import multiprocessing as mp
import os
import sys


def run_case(m: int, n: int, k: int, bias_enabled: bool) -> None:
    import torch
    import flashinfer

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    a = torch.randn((m, k), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

    # mm_bf16 expects B as shape [k, n] with B.T contiguous.
    b_storage = torch.randn((n, k), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    b = b_storage.t()

    bias = None
    if bias_enabled:
        bias = torch.randn((n,), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(
        "running",
        {"m": m, "n": n, "k": k, "bias": bias_enabled},
        flush=True,
    )
    out = flashinfer.mm_bf16(
        a,
        b,
        bias=bias,
        pdl=False,
        backend="tinygemm",
    )
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("done", out.shape, out.dtype, flush=True)


def main() -> int:
    cases = [
        # Observed watchdog hangs in a single-layer benchmark.
        (1, 7168, 5120, False),
        (1, 55296, 5120, False),
        (1, 5120, 27648, True),
        (8192, 5120, 27648, False),
    ]
    for case in cases:
        p = mp.Process(target=run_case, args=case)
        p.start()
        p.join(timeout=30)
        if p.is_alive():
            print("HANG", case, flush=True)
            p.kill()
            p.join()
            return 1
        if p.exitcode:
            print("FAILED", case, "exitcode", p.exitcode, flush=True)
            return p.exitcode
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mp.set_start_method("spawn", force=True)
    raise SystemExit(main())
```

Expected: each call should either complete or return a regular Python/CUDA error.

Actual: at least some cases hang until the subprocess is killed.

## Additional evidence from a larger single-layer sweep

The local benchmark key format is:

```text
backend,pdl,bias,m,n,k
```

Examples of explicit TinyGEMM cells that the watchdog killed:

```text
STUCK on 'tinygemm,False,False,8192,5120,27648'
STUCK on 'tinygemm,False,True,1,5120,27648'
STUCK on 'tinygemm,False,False,1,55296,5120'
STUCK on 'tinygemm,False,False,1,7168,5120'
STUCK on 'tinygemm,False,True,1024,7168,5120'
```

We also saw `backend="auto"` / vLLM `vllm-auto` hangs on the same family of large-N / large-K shapes. In those cases the process was stuck under the autotuner profiling path:

```text
mm_bf16
  bf16_gemm_sm100
    AutoTuner.choose_one
      _profile_single_kernel
        pure_profile
          torch.cuda.Stream.synchronize  # never returns
```

The candidate ops loaded before the autotune wedge included:

```text
mm_bf16_cublaslt, bf16_gemm_cutlass, tgv_gemm_bf16, tinygemm2, trtllm_utils
```

We cannot prove from the auto-path stack alone which candidate is always responsible, but explicit `backend="tinygemm"` hangs on overlapping shapes make TinyGEMM a strong suspect. As a local mitigation, excluding `tinygemm` from BF16 `backend="auto"` candidates avoids exposing vLLM's BF16 FlashInfer autotune path to this hang.

## Notes

TinyGEMM is described as a small-M BF16 GEMM backend, but the current hard requirement checks allow some large projection shapes through. It may be safer for TinyGEMM to reject unsupported / out-of-design-range shapes before launch, or for BF16 auto selection to avoid TinyGEMM on these shapes.

records.title: Feature request: honor KV pool `stride(0)` in `trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4`
records.body:
The DSV4 sparse decode launcher treats the paged KV pool as contiguous along the page dimension and discards its actual `stride(0)`. It should gather against the tensor's real leading stride, so callers can pass strided pools — a slice of a larger buffer, or several pools sharing one per-block allocation.

**Current behavior** — `trtllm_paged_attention_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4` (`flashinfer/data/csrc/trtllm_fmha_kernel_launcher.cu`:
```cpp
int const sparse_page_size       = 1;
int const kv_stride_keys_values  = primary_kv_cache.stride(-2) * stride_idx_factor;  // per-token stride
int const sparse_kv_stride_batch = kv_stride_keys_values;                            // page stride := per-token stride
```

`sparse_indices` are flat physical token positions. Forcing `page_size = 1` and `kv_stride_batch = per-token stride` collapses the gather to `base + sparse_indices[i] * per_token_stride`, so `primary_kv_cache.stride(0)` is never read (`sliding_window_kv_cache` is passed pointer-only and inherits the same strides). This is exact only when the page dim is tightly packed (`stride(0) == size(-2) * stride(-2)`); otherwise every token in page ≥ 1 resolves into the wrong block. There is no contiguity guard, so a strided pool is silently miscomputed rather than rejected.

**Requested** — decompose each index against the real page size and fold the leading stride into the address:

```
page, tok = divmod(sparse_indices[i], primary_kv_cache.size(-2))
addr      = base + page * kv.stride(0) + tok * per_token_stride
```

and read `sliding_window_kv_cache`'s own strides. Both precedents are already in-tree: the dense launcher (`trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache`, ~L351) sources `kv_stride_batch = key_cache.stride(0)`, and FlashMLA's sparse decode does the equivalent `divmod`-by-`page_block_size`. The sparse DSV4 path is the outlier.

**Motivation** — unblocks the packed DSV4 KV layout in [vllm-project/vllm#44577](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44577), which coalesces the DSV4 components (compressed-KV, sliding-window, indexer) into one shared per-block allocation and hands each to the backend as a strided view, so per-component `stride(0)` is the full per-block span. Today that layout decodes against the wrong blocks (gsm8k ~95% → ~0% in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47783); honoring `stride(0)` lets it feed the kernel directly, without a per-component contiguous repack on the hot path.

**Secondary (defect)** — even if strided support is deferred, a contiguity check on both pools would turn today's silent corruption into a fast, clear failure.

**Env** — FlashInfer `0.6.13`, Blackwell (sm100), via vLLM `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4`.
records.author: majunze2001

records.title: Split flashinfer-jit-cache to keep h512 AOT kernels installable
records.body:
#3769 showed the practical packaging problem: including FA2 `(512, 512)` kernels in the default `flashinfer-jit-cache` wheel can push release assets over the GitHub upload limit. At the same time, keeping h512 JIT-only is painful for users serving large-head models, because the kernels need to be compiled again when the cache is not already warm.

Splitting the JIT cache by feature/head dimension would fix this.

For example:

```text
flashinfer-jit-cache
  default/common AOT kernels

flashinfer-jit-cache-fa2-h512
  optional FA2 head_dim=(512,512) AOT kernels
```

Users who need h512, for example vLLM users serving large-head models, could install the optional package:

```bash
pip install flashinfer-jit-cache
pip install flashinfer-jit-cache-fa2-h512
```

The loader would need to search multiple installed cache package roots:

1. default `flashinfer-jit-cache`
2. optional `flashinfer-jit-cache-fa2-h512`
3. normal JIT fallback if no prebuilt kernel is found

This keeps the default package within the release asset limit, and h512 users can opt in to prebuilt kernels.

records.title: [Bug] trtllm-gen spec-as-decode (q_len_per_req=8) with BF16 query + FP8 KV cache silently mis-computes sliding-window attention on SM100
records.body:
## Summary

`trtllm-gen` spec-as-decode (`trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` with `q_len_per_req=8`) with **BF16 query + FP8 KV cache** silently mis-computes **sliding-window** attention on SM100 (B200) once `seq_len > window`. The corruption is severe (max abs err ~0.8–1.8 on outputs of magnitude ~1–3, cosine down to 0.93 vs reference) but *localized*: typically a single (query-row, head) pair per failing call, and only at some `seq_len` values (data-dependent).

Controls on the exact same inputs are all clean:
- **FP8 query** at the same (seed, seq_len): max err ~0.02 (quant noise) — clean
- **window off** (`window_left=-1`): max err ~0.004 — clean
- `q_len_per_req` 1/2/4: clean in the tested grid
- seq_len ≤ window: clean

Because the error is silent and localized, in end-to-end serving it manifests as sporadic wrong tokens / short repetition loops rather than a crash — easy to mistake for model behavior.

## Environment

- flashinfer-python **0.6.14** (latest release; flashinfer-cubin 0.6.13), torch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13
- NVIDIA B200 (SM100), driver 580.x
- Geometry from gemma-4-31B: `head_dim=256`, 32 q heads, 16 kv heads, `sm_scale=1.0`, `window_left=1023`, `page_size=16`, HND

## Repro

```python
import torch
from flashinfer.decode import trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache

DEV = "cuda"
FP8 = torch.float8_e4m3fn

def torch_ref(q, k, v, sm_scale, window_left, qlen):
    total = k.shape[0]
    hq, hk = q.shape[1], k.shape[1]
    rep = hq // hk
    kr = k.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1).float().permute(1, 0, 2)
    vr = v.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1).float().permute(1, 0, 2)
    qf = q.float().permute(1, 0, 2)
    logits = torch.bmm(qf, kr.transpose(1, 2)) * sm_scale
    qpos = torch.arange(total - qlen, total, device=q.device)
    kpos = torch.arange(total, device=q.device)
    mask = kpos[None, :] <= qpos[:, None]
    if window_left >= 0:
        mask = mask & (kpos[None, :] >= (qpos[:, None] - window_left))
    logits = logits.masked_fill(~mask[None], float("-inf"))
    return torch.bmm(torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1), vr).permute(1, 0, 2)

def run_case(total_len, qlen, q_fp8, window_left, page=16, hq=32, hk=16, hd=256,
             sm=1.0, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    n_pages = (total_len + page - 1) // page
    q = torch.randn(qlen, hq, hd, device=DEV, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.5
    k = torch.randn(total_len, hk, hd, device=DEV, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.5
    v = torch.randn(total_len, hk, hd, device=DEV, dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.5
    k_store, v_store = k.to(FP8), v.to(FP8)
    k_eff, v_eff = k_store.to(torch.bfloat16), v_store.to(torch.bfloat16)
    cache = torch.zeros(n_pages, 2, hk, page, hd, device=DEV, dtype=FP8)
    for p in range(n_pages):
        lo, hi = p * page, min((p + 1) * page, total_len)
        cache[p, 0, :, : hi - lo] = k_store[lo:hi].permute(1, 0, 2)
        cache[p, 1, :, : hi - lo] = v_store[lo:hi].permute(1, 0, 2)
    q_in = q.to(FP8) if q_fp8 else q
    ws = torch.zeros(256 * 1024 * 1024, dtype=torch.uint8, device=DEV)
    out = trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache(
        query=q_in, kv_cache=cache, workspace_buffer=ws,
        block_tables=torch.arange(n_pages, dtype=torch.int32, device=DEV).unsqueeze(0),
        seq_lens=torch.tensor([total_len], dtype=torch.int32, device=DEV),
        max_seq_len=total_len, bmm1_scale=sm, bmm2_scale=1.0,
        window_left=window_left,
        out=torch.empty(qlen, hq, hd, device=DEV, dtype=torch.bfloat16),
        kv_layout="HND", backend="trtllm-gen", q_len_per_req=qlen,
    )
    ref = torch_ref(q_in.to(torch.bfloat16), k_eff, v_eff, sm, window_left, qlen)
    err = (out.float() - ref).abs()
    cos = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(
        out.float().flatten(1), ref.flatten(1), dim=1)
    return err, cos

for q_fp8 in (False, True):
    for wl in (1023, -1):
        for seed, total in ((0, 1286), (0, 2053), (2, 2053)):
            err, cos = run_case(total, 8, q_fp8, wl, seed=seed)
            print(f"q={'fp8' if q_fp8 else 'bf16'} wl={wl:5d} seed={seed} "
                  f"seq={total}: max_err={err.max():.4f} min_cos={cos.min():.3f}")
```

Output on B200 / flashinfer 0.6.14:

```
q=bf16 wl= 1023 seed=0 seq=1286: max_err=1.3916 min_cos=0.935   <-- BROKEN
q=bf16 wl= 1023 seed=0 seq=2053: max_err=1.7756 min_cos=0.937   <-- BROKEN
q=bf16 wl= 1023 seed=2 seq=2053: max_err=0.9783 min_cos=0.977   <-- BROKEN
q=bf16 wl=   -1 seed=0 seq=1286: max_err=0.0039 min_cos=1.000
q=bf16 wl=   -1 seed=0 seq=2053: max_err=0.0039 min_cos=1.000
q=bf16 wl=   -1 seed=2 seq=2053: max_err=0.0039 min_cos=1.000
q=fp8  wl= 1023 seed=0 seq=1286: max_err=0.0255 min_cos=1.000
q=fp8  wl= 1023 seed=0 seq=2053: max_err=0.0282 min_cos=1.000
q=fp8  wl= 1023 seed=2 seq=2053: max_err=0.0165 min_cos=1.000
q=fp8  wl=   -1 ...                                clean
```

Error structure at (seed=0, seq=1286): per-query-row max err `[0.004, 1.392, 0.011, 0.086, 0.007, 0.004, 0.004, 0.003]` — row 1 only, and within that row only head 24 exceeds 0.25. This looks like one KV tile near the window boundary being mis-handled (skipped/mis-masked) for a subset of CTAs in the BF16-Q × FP8-KV sliding-window spec-decode kernel variant.

More observations from a wider sweep:
- Sporadic in `seq_len`: e.g. at `wl=1023, qlen=8` seeds 0–2 over seq 1024–2080, failures at 1286 and 2053; at `wl=127` failures at seq 136, 137, 141, 142 (err up to 1.4).
- `page_size=32`: no failures in the same scan; `page_size=64`: fails at seq 1031 (err 1.33, cos 0.953) — page-size-dependent.
- Repeat-run deterministic (same inputs → bitwise same wrong output), and content-invariant across rows — it is a fixed indexing/predicate defect, not a race.

## End-to-end impact

Found via vLLM: serving gemma-4-31B (50/60 layers SWA window 1024) with MTP speculative decoding (verify = spec-as-decode `q_len_per_req=8`), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` and `--attention-config '{"disable_flashinfer_q_quantization": true}'` (BF16-Q) produces sporadic corrupted tokens and short repetition loops in otherwise coherent output, e.g. "Instead of instead of instead of instead (of using a blocking two-phase commit)". The same server without the flag (FP8-Q), or with the flag but without speculation (q_len_per_req=1), is clean. vLLM issue: (link to follow in a comment)

records.title: FlashInfer MNNVL twoshotAllreduceKernel write out-of-bounds → Xid 31 UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT, whole-node GPU hang requires physical machine reboot
records.body:
## Summary

An sglang service serving GLM-5.2-NVFP4 (TP=4, using MNNVL all-reduce) triggered an out-of-bounds global write (Warp Illegal Address) in `flashinfer::trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce::twoshotAllreduceKernel` during the tensor-parallel all-reduce stage. This caused a GPU MMU Fault (Xid 31, `UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT`) that propagated through the NVLink fabric to all 8 GPUs on the node. The driver was unable to isolate the fault locally and the GPU graphics engine was wedged. **Restarting the pod / sglang process / `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset` all failed; only a physical machine reboot could recover.**

- Kernel implementation: FlashInfer (version 0.6.12)
- Caller: sglang (dev build `0.0.0.dev1+g22dce5720`)
- Algorithm origin: TensorRT-LLM's MNNVL all-reduce (namespace named after the source)
- Compilation: TVM (compiler only; runtime is self-contained)

---

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Node | `36.0.4.36` |
| GPU | 8 × NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC (GB110GL-B, sm_103) |
| Driver | 580.82.07 (Open Kernel Module) |
| CUDA | 13.0 (cuda-gdb 13.0) |
| Container | Privileged (`privileged: true`, CapEff 41/41 all set, `IPC_LOCK`+`SYS_PTRACE`, `hostNetwork: true`) |
| Model | GLM-5.2-NVFP4, TP=4 |
| Service | sglang `0.0.0.dev1+g22dce5720` |
| flashinfer | `flashinfer-python-0.6.12+cu130` |
| Key launch args | `--tp 4 --cuda-graph-max-bs 64 --max-running-requests 64 --speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 5 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 --enable-hierarchical-cache ... --crash-dump-folder /tmp/crashdump` |
| Comm stack | MNNVL all-reduce + NVSHMEM (`NVSHMEM_IB_*`) + Mooncake RDMA (`MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL=rdma`) |
| Coredump trigger | `CUDA_ENABLE_COREDUMP_ON_EXCEPTION=1`, `CUDA_COREDUMP_FILE=/tmp/crashdump/cuda_coredump_%h.%p.%t` (hostPath persisted to host `/data0/sglang/crashdump`) |

---

## Symptoms & Timeline

```
19:14:43  Xid 13  GPU (PCI:1a:00)  Graphics Exception               ← 1st crash (1 GPU)
19:15:34-39  Xid 31 × 8 GPUs  MMU Fault: UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT         ← 2nd crash (all 8, within 5s)
19:23:14  Host kernel reboot (derived from /proc/uptime)
19:24:01  nvidia kernel module reloaded (/sys/module/nvidia mtime)
19:24:03  8 GPUs re-enumerated in the same second (/proc/driver/nvidia/gpus creation time)
19:25:16  Pod restarted, service recovered
```

12 CUDA coredumps were generated in `/tmp/crashdump/`, in two batches:
- 19:10 (ts 1783421884/1885): 5 dumps
- 19:15 (ts 1783422676/2678): 7 dumps
- Covering all TP ranks (filename `%p` = sglang scheduler PIDs 148/149/150/151)

After recovery the node is stable, no new coredumps, `restartCount=0`.

---

## Direct Cause (confirmed via CUDA coredumps)

Loaded all 12 coredumps with `cuda-gdb` (`target cudacore <dump>` command) — **all identical**:

- Exception type: **`CUDA Exception: Warp Illegal Address`**
- Faulting kernel: `flashinfer::trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce::twoshotAllreduceKernel<(unsigned char)4, __nv_bfloat16, float4>` (template arg `4` corresponds to `--tp 4`)
- Trigger instruction (kernel offset `+0x14F0`, i.e. `errorpc`):
  ```
  /*14f0*/   STG.E.128  desc[UR14][R6.64], R8      // 128-bit global store, writing reduce result back
  ```
- grid/block: `<<<(384,6,1),(128,1,1)>>>`
- All 12 dumps: same kernel, same `errorpc`; only absolute addresses differ due to per-process base addresses.

### SASS analysis (read succeeds / write fails)

Same descriptor `UR14` (loaded from kernel arg via `LDCU.64 UR14, c[0x0][0x358]`):

- **Read stage** (STRONG.SYS cross-node reads, before the write) **succeeded**, did not fault:
  ```
  /*0d80*/  LDG.E.128.STRONG.SYS R8,  desc[UR14][R6.64]
  /*0d90*/  LDG.E.128.STRONG.SYS R12, desc[UR14][R28.64]
  /*0da0*/  LDG.E.128.STRONG.SYS R16, desc[UR14][R30.64]
  /*0db0*/  LDG.E.128.STRONG.SYS R24, desc[UR14][R32.64]
  ```
- **Write-back offset computation chain**:
  ```
  /*1480*/  IMAD.U32       R6, RZ, RZ, UR12          //  R6 = UR12 (uniform param)
  /*14a0*/  IMAD           R19, R2, UR25, R19        //  R19 = R2*UR25 + R19  (R2=2)
  /*14d0*/  IMAD.WIDE.U32  R6, R19, 0x10, R6        //  R6 = R19*16 + UR12
  /*14f0*/  STG.E.128  desc[UR14][R6.64], R8         //  ← out-of-bounds write
  ```
- Faulting warp register snapshot: write offset `R6 = 0x1b49200` (28.6 MB); read-stage registers `R28=0xbc064000`, `R30=0xba8a8000` are valid GPU memory addresses.

**Conclusion**: descriptor `UR14` is valid (reads succeeded); the fault is an **out-of-bounds write-back offset**, not a global peer-mapping failure. The offset is computed via `(R2*UR25+R19)*16 + UR12` from uniform index params (`UR12`, `UR25`) and `R2` — suspected mismatch between tokenDim/rank/Lamport buffer layout and the actual request size.

> Note: UR (uniform registers) are captured as 0 in the coredump (uniform state not captured by coredump); the read-stage success proves UR14 was actually non-zero. Real UR12/UR25 must be captured via live cuda-gdb.

---

## Hardware-level Classification (confirmed via `/var/log/kern.log`)

```
19:14:43  NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:1a:00): 13, Graphics Exception: ESR 0x57e7b0=0x81e0017 0x57e7b4=0x24 0x57e7a8=0x1f81fb60 0x57e7ac=0x1174
19:15:34  NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:9a:00): 31, pid=477445, name=python3, channel 0x00000002, intr 00000000.
          MMU Fault: ENGINE GRAPHICS GPC0 UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT faulted @ 0x182400_0030198d.
          Fault is of type UNRECOGNIZED_FAULT UNRECOGNIZED_ACCESS_TYPE
19:15:34  Xid 31 PCI:0000:f0:00 pid=477448 ... UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT ...
19:15:35  Xid 31 PCI:0000:bd:00 pid=477446 ... UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT ...
19:15:36  Xid 31 PCI:0000:df:00 pid=477447 ... UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT ...
19:15:37  Xid 31 PCI:0000:73:00 pid=477782 ...
19:15:37  Xid 31 PCI:0000:62:00 pid=477781 ...
19:15:37  Xid 31 PCI:0000:40:00 pid=477780 ...
19:15:39  Xid 31 PCI:0000:1a:00 pid=477779 ...
19:24:03  NVRM: loading NVIDIA UNIX Open Kernel Module for x86_64 580.82.07  (after host reboot)
```

**Key classification: Xid 31 + `UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT`**

- Normal Xid 31 MMU Fault: driver recognizes the client → destroys that channel → local isolation, container restart recovers.
- `UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT`: MMU received the access but **cannot identify the client** →
  - client context corrupted beyond driver recognition;
  - driver has no handle to destroy, cannot isolate locally;
  - the faulting client remains attached to the GPU graphics engine, keeps issuing illegal accesses, wedging the engine;
  - `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset` precondition (no active client) unsatisfied → reset also fails.

**Fabric propagation evidence**: all 8 GPUs reported Xid 31 within 5 seconds, across 8 different PIDs (477445-477782), belonging to multiple independent pods on the same node (`one-9`, `two-5`, `mooncake-store-9`). A single pod's OOB propagated through the NVLink fabric to the whole-node GPU interconnect domain → multiple pods on the same node crashed simultaneously.

---

## Why pod / sglang restart cannot recover (confirmed)

1. **Shared kernel driver**: the pod is privileged and shares the single nvidia kernel driver with the host. GPU command queues, MMU, and client state live in the host kernel-mode driver; the container has no independent driver instance.
2. **Fault is outside the container isolation boundary**: Linux namespaces isolate PID/network/mount/IPC, **not GPUs**. Xid 31 `UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT` is in the GPU hardware + host driver layer, outside the recoverable scope of container namespaces (privileged or not — equally powerless).
3. **Client cannot be detached**: process exit does not auto-clean the residual client on the GPU (driver can't recognize it, can't reclaim it); `--gpu-reset` fails on the unsatisfied precondition → deadlock; only a host reboot can zero the state at the hardware layer.

**Conclusion**: "must reboot the physical machine" is virtually the only recovery path for this fault at the hardware level — not an operator shortcoming.

---

## Responsibility Boundaries & Call Chain (confirmed)

### Call chain
```
sglang (Python, tensor-parallel all-reduce)
  └─ calls flashinfer's trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce op
     └─ flashinfer Python binding → tvm::ffi
        └─ trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce_fusion()  (TVM-compiled host function)
           └─ launch: flashinfer::trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce::twoshotAllreduceKernel<4,bf16,float4>
              └─ (TVM-compiled cubin, self-contained, no libnvinfer/libtvm runtime dependency)
                 └─ MNNVL two-shot reduce over NVLink fabric
                    └─ ✗ STG.E.128 write OOB → Xid 31
```

### Ownership by layer

| Layer | Owner | Responsibility | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Algorithm design | TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA) | MNNVL all-reduce algorithm origin | `nv_internal/tensorrt_llm/` reference dir |
| **Kernel implementation** | **FlashInfer 0.6.12** | write-back offset / buffer layout in `twoshotAllreduceKernel` | source `flashinfer/data/include/flashinfer/comm/trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.cuh` line 761 |
| Compilation | TVM | compiler only, self-contained product | `.so` does not link libtvm/libnvinfer (`ldd` confirmed) |
| Integration/caller | sglang (dev build) | params/buffer size passed to kernel | caller, decides tokenDim/buffer |

### Key source locations
- `.cu` (JIT entry): `flashinfer/data/csrc/trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.cu`
  - top: `using namespace flashinfer::trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce;`
  - defines `trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce_fusion(TensorView input, int64_t multicast_buffer_ptr, ...)`
  - includes `flashinfer/comm/trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.cuh` + `tvm_ffi_utils.h`
- `.cuh` (kernel body): `flashinfer/data/include/flashinfer/comm/trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.cuh` (1223 lines)
  - line 30: `namespace trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce {`
  - line 761: `__global__ __launch_bounds__(128) void twoshotAllreduceKernel(...)`
  - includes: only CUDA standard headers + flashinfer's own `utils.cuh`/`logging.h`, **no nv_internal/tensorrt_llm**

### `.so` dependencies (`ldd` confirmed)
```
libcudart.so.13, libcuda.so.1, libstdc++.so.6, libm/libc/libgcc_s/libdl/libpthread/librt
```
Does not link `libnvinfer` / `libtvm` → kernel binary is self-contained; no TRT-LLM / TVM runtime dependency.

---

## Responsibility Attribution (needs reproduction to confirm)

Whether the bug is in FlashInfer or sglang requires reproducing with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` + cuda-gdb attached, printing the kernel's input params at the faulting warp:

- If `tokenDim * sizeof(T)` exceeds sglang's pre-allocated all-reduce buffer → **sglang passes OOB params** (integration layer)
- If params are valid but the kernel computes the address off the range → **FlashInfer kernel bug** (implementation layer)

---

## Trigger Cause (not yet located; needs investigation)

The direct cause is an OOB all-reduce write-back offset, but the **trigger condition is not yet confirmed**. Need to check the sglang request load on node `36.0.4.36` around the crash time (19:10-19:15):

- Whether request tensor shape / sequence length exceeds the pre-allocated all-reduce buffer capacity;
- Whether the number of tokens produced by EAGLE speculative decoding (`--speculative-num-draft-tokens 6`) is consistent with buffer config;
- Match between `--cuda-graph-max-bs 64` / `--max-running-requests 64` and actual load;
- Whether the NVSHMEM symmetric memory (global segment) registration range covers the kernel's actual access offset `R6=0x1b49200`.

---

## Reproduction Status

**Currently unable to fully reproduce**, reasons:

1. No hardware: B300 + NVLink fabric + NVSHMEM/MNNVL stack (analysis env has no GPU).
2. No trigger condition: the cause is not located, cannot deliberately construct OOB input.
3. Unacceptable cost: once triggered it wedges the whole-node GPU and requires a host reboot; should not be induced in shared/production environments.

A controlled path that can progress (no hardware, zero risk → requires a controllable B300 test machine):

1. **Static analysis**: read `twoshotAllreduceKernel` line by line, derive the OOB boundary of `R6 = (R2*UR25+R19)*16 + UR12`, produce a hypothesis of "what input goes OOB".
2. **Log correlation**: fetch sglang request logs at crash time, verify the hypothesis.
3. **Controlled reproduction**: based on the hypothesis, write a minimal repro script and run on a dedicated rebootable B300 test machine, trying small-scale to trigger the illegal address first (may only coredump without wedging).

> Note: even at small scale, an MNNVL OOB may still propagate via fabric and wedge the GPU; step 3 must run on a dedicated rebootable test machine.

---

## Mitigation & Improvement

1. **Stop-gap**: consider temporarily disabling / downgrading the MNNVL all-reduce path to plain NCCL all-reduce (perf loss but avoids whole-node hang).
2. **Alerting**: configure real-time alerts for Xid 13 / 31 (especially `UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT`).
3. **Log persistence**: ensure host journald `Storage=persistent` or remote syslog, so similar investigations don't depend on manually grepping `/var/log/kern.log` (this case relied on kern.log to confirm the Xid type).
4. **Root-cause fix**:
   - FlashInfer: bounds-check the write-back offset in `twoshotAllreduceKernel`;
   - sglang: verify all-reduce buffer capacity vs request shape / EAGLE token count consistency.

---

## Key Evidence Checklist (for upstream triage)

- [x] 12 coredumps consistent: `Warp Illegal Address` + `twoshotAllreduceKernel<4,bf16,float4>` + `errorpc +0x14F0`
- [x] SASS trigger instruction: `STG.E.128 desc[UR14][R6.64], R8` (OOB write, read stage succeeded)
- [x] kern.log: `Xid 13` (19:14) → `Xid 31 × 8 GPUs UNRECOGNIZED_CLIENT` (19:15)
- [x] Host-reboot ironclad: `/proc/uptime` + `/sys/module/nvidia` mtime (19:24:01) + kern.log `NVRM loading` (19:24:03), three-way consistent
- [x] Kernel source located: `flashinfer/.../trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.cuh:761`
- [x] No TRT-LLM/TVM runtime dependency at runtime (`ldd` confirmed)
- [ ] Crash-time request load logs (to do, for locating the trigger)
- [ ] Repro script (to do, needs B300 test env)

---

## Where to File

- **Primary**: FlashInfer — `github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer`
  File: `csrc/comm/trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.cuh` (or the include-path equivalent), function `twoshotAllreduceKernel` (line 761)
  Version: flashinfer 0.6.12
- **Secondary**: sglang — `github.com/sgl-project/sglang`
  Version: `0.0.0.dev1+g22dce5720` (dev build; confirm whether it contains unreleased fixes / customizations)
- TVM (compiler only, low responsibility unless a codegen bug)
- TensorRT-LLM (algorithm origin only, no runtime involvement, low responsibility)

records.title: [Feature] Warn or raise when wrapper run() is captured in a CUDA graph without use_cuda_graph=True
records.body:
Capturing `run()` on a default-mode wrapper (e.g. `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` constructed with `use_cuda_graph=False`) and replaying after `plan()` silently returns wrong output, then an illegal memory access as sequences grow. Default-mode plan buffers aren't persistent, so this is documented-unsupported — but the failure mode is silent corruption that presents as a model-quality problem rather than API misuse. It cost us days in vLLM: near-zero speculative-decoding acceptance on Blackwell before we traced it to a captured non-CG-mode prefill wrapper (fixed downstream in vllm-project/vllm#48167).

A `torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing()` check in `run()` when `use_cuda_graph=False` would make the misuse fail loudly at capture time.

(Observed with flashinfer 0.6.13, fa2 backend, B300/SM103, but the contract is arch-independent.)

Happy to PR the guard if you'd take it.

records.title: [Bug] TRTLLM-GEN MLA rejects valid native-width block tables and forces padding
records.body:
## Problem

`trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(..., backend="trtllm-gen")`
currently requires the block-table width to satisfy:

```python
block_num % (128 / page_size) == 0
```

The TRTLLM-GEN launcher itself accepts the native block-table width: it reads
`block_tables.size(-1)` and forwards that value as the maximum pages per KV
sequence. The public-API validation therefore forces callers to pad otherwise
valid page tables.

For example, with `page_size=32` and `max_seq_len=1025`, the native width is
33. That width is valid for TRTLLM-GEN but is rejected because it is not
divisible by four.

## Performance impact

This surfaced while investigating a TensorRT-LLM B300 MLA decode regression
(NVBUG 6430674). Padding the page table during CUDA-graph capture introduced
one fill and one copy node per MLA invocation.

Removing the unnecessary padding in the caller:

- eliminated 4,096 fill kernels and 4,096 copy kernels from the measured trace
- removed exactly 8,192 CUDA-graph nodes
- improved output throughput from 5,125.14 to 5,220.09 tokens/s (`+1.85%`)
- reduced stable graph makespan from 18.467885 ms to 18.051944 ms (`-2.25%`)

## Expected behavior

When the caller explicitly selects `backend="trtllm-gen"`, the public API
should accept the native block-table width.

Rank, shared/separate page-index layout, dtype, device, and batch-size
validation should remain unchanged. Other backends should retain their current
width-alignment behavior.

records.title: [RFC] Autotuner v2: FlashInfer-managed persistent cache and deployment-matched measurement
records.body:
**Status**: MVP implemented in #3861 (opt-in, v1 untouched). This RFC covers the design, the evidence behind it, and the roadmap; feedback wanted before we start migrating frameworks.

## Summary

FlashInfer should own the persistence and compatibility rules for its autotuning results. Frameworks such as vLLM and SGLang should decide *when* to warm up and how to coordinate distributed workers — but they should not construct FlashInfer cache keys, interpret its JSON schema, or manage cache files, as they do today.

The proposal has four parts:

1. **A managed persistent cache** (`autotune_v2()`): environment-hashed directories, one atomic entry per tuned operation, invalid entries are misses (never errors), old generations left on disk.
2. **A measurement policy** (`MeasurementPolicy`): tune the way you deploy — eager vs CUDA-graph execution as the primary axis, cold-L2 as a secondary one.
3. **A runner contract**: rules that make "serving executes the tactic the tuner chose" structurally guaranteed rather than convention-enforced.
4. **An accuracy harness**: tuner quality ("picks the fastest tactic") becomes a measured claim (regret vs. an oracle), not an assumption.

Autotune data is a disposable performance optimization. Cross-version cache migration is a non-goal: after an upgrade, paying the tuning cost once for the new environment is acceptable. This follows the compiler-cache patterns of Triton and `torch.compile`/Inductor: key artifacts by program + compiler + environment, publish atomically, treat unusable entries as work to rebuild, own the local cache, and expose only an opaque export/import boundary.

## Evidence 1: how frameworks actually use v1

A survey of vLLM and SGLang (HEAD, 2026-07) shows both use exactly one pattern — **one-shot startup warmup around a whole-model dummy forward, before CUDA-graph capture; serving always runs outside any context**:

- **vLLM**: rank 0 runs `autotune(tune_mode=True, cache=<path>)`, broadcasts the raw JSON file bytes, every rank atomically rewrites the file and calls `load_configs(path)`. The cache path is a vLLM-computed `sha256(compile-factors)` directory — vLLM had to reinvent cache hashing, atomic writes, and an enable knob.
- **SGLang**: every rank tunes simultaneously (the dummy forward contains collectives, so rank-0-only tuning deadlocks DeepEP), with **one JSON file per rank**, its own model/quant/parallelism hash, its own disable env.
- **Features with zero external use**: `tune_mode=False` in serving, `tuning_buckets`, `round_up`, direct `save_configs`, `FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNER_LOAD_FROM_FILE` (the last has been silently broken since #3367 with zero reports — confirming zero users). `skip_ops` has latent demand (vllm-project/vllm#46238 wants per-op exclusion; SGLang disables autotune entirely for some models because one op crashes).
- **Exhibit A for key completeness**: vllm-project/vllm#43119 — the v1 file cache missed `use_8x4_sf_layout` in its key, invalid tactics were replayed, and vLLM **disabled the persistent cache for all multi-rank deployments** (still disabled on the general path today, even after the flashinfer-side fix in #3367). A single key-completeness bug cost the feature its default.

Implications used throughout: reuse must not require an active context; the hashing/broadcast/knob code both frameworks built is exactly the policy FlashInfer should own; concurrent all-ranks tuning must be safe; key completeness needs a contract, not vigilance.

## Evidence 2: what field issues say

An audit of open autotuner-related issues clusters them into buckets; this RFC addresses the first four:

| bucket | issues | how this RFC addresses it |
|---|---|---|
| cross-rank tactic divergence | #3186, #3537 | shared store + planned rank-consistency step; composes with #3187 (see distributed section) |
| tuned tactic slower than default | #3537, #3622, #3409 | accuracy harness diagnoses; planned regression guard (default path always races as a candidate) |
| stale/invalid tactic at execute time | #3566 (mitigated by #3437), vllm#43119 | runner contract rules 1/4/5; environment-fingerprint invalidation |
| measurement ≠ deployment | #3648, #3719 | `MeasurementPolicy(execution_mode=...)` |
| probe-tensor crashes | #3558, #3569, #3085 | `skip_ops` quarantine is the mitigation; root fixes are separate work |
| kernel/candidate coverage (SM120 etc.) | #2992, #3119, #2577 | out of scope (kernel-side); harness quantifies the cost |

Notably, none of the open issues complains about v1's persistence file itself — the field pain is consistency, selection quality, and validity. That is why measurement policy and the runner contract are first-class parts of this proposal rather than afterthoughts.

## Limitations of the v1 cache (brief)

The caller owns too much FlashInfer-specific policy (filename choice = cache identity); environment mismatch is awkward (whole file rejected, refuses to save back); a monolithic JSON is a poor concurrent-update unit (read/merge/write races; one corrupt file kills every entry); the namespace is coarser than the data (model-level filename prevents op-level reuse); integer tactic indices are not stable identities (#3707 is the focused correctness patch for that; orthogonal to and composable with this proposal).

## Design

### API: a standalone `autotune_v2()` entry point

v2 is deliberately a separate context manager, not new parameters on `autotune()` — v1 stays byte-identical, and the eventual v1 removal is a clean deletion instead of a subtle behavior change:

```python
with flashinfer.autotune_v2(
    mode="tune",               # "tune" (profile misses + publish) | "replay" (serve tuned winners)
    persistent_cache=True,     # touch disk at all?
    cache_root=None,           # placement-only ROOT DIRECTORY (not identity)
    measure=None,              # MeasurementPolicy, see below
):
    model(dummy_inputs)        # warmup forward; tuning is a side effect
```

`mode` names a positive action, not a negated flag — `mode="replay"` is the serving path (replay tuned winners, no profiling), which does *not* read like "throw away the tuning results" the way a `enable_tuning=False` boolean did. `persistent_cache` stays as the orthogonal disk toggle:

| `mode` | `persistent_cache` | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `"tune"` | True *(default)* | tune misses, publish to disk |
| `"tune"` | False | tune in-memory only (disk-forbidden environments) |
| `"replay"` | True | serve from the on-disk cache (no profiling) |
| `"replay"` | False | no-op unless already hydrated |

**Attach semantics** (the key lifecycle decision, forced by the survey): `persistent_cache=True` attaches the store for the remainder of the process; the context scopes only *when profiling cost may be paid*. Both frameworks serve outside any context — a context-scoped store would silently regress serving to heuristics after warmup exits. Tune-on-first-call (Triton-style) is deliberately rejected for serving: latency jitter, collective deadlocks, must-precede-graph-capture, profiling OOM risk.

**One process, one ambient policy.** Ambient attach is action-at-a-distance — a bare `model(x)` uses whatever policy was last attached — but it is architecturally forced, not a stylistic choice: serving replays a captured CUDA graph (no Python runs at replay), and the autotuned ops are buried in layer forwards, so the tactic must be pre-resolved and read from process-global state with no context in scope. The idiomatic `with` belongs to *tuning* (a real scoped window, which warmup uses); serving is unavoidably context-free. Consequently `autotune_v2` does **not** nest (v2-in-v2 fails fast) and there is no per-region scoped-override knob: a process serves under one ambient policy (last-wins across sequential warmup contexts). This was validated against both consumers — vLLM and SGLang each open exactly one warmup context and then serve bare — so the removed machinery (a store stack, a `scope=` dimension) supported only a use case with no user.

**Mixed-mode (verified against vLLM + SGLang, current main).** Both frameworks *do* run the same autotuned op both eager and under CUDA-graph capture in one process at default settings, and this is the intended steady state, not transitional: decode runs under a FULL graph while large prefill (>~512 tokens in vLLM; MLA/MoE-A2A/DP prefill in SGLang) runs eager, and the autotune warmup forward itself is forced eager. **But it does not create a serving-time winner collision**: prefill (large M = num_tokens) and decode (small M = batch size) land in disjoint shape buckets, so the store's per-`(op, bucket)` entries are each served in one consistent mode. So FlashInfer does *not* need per-bucket dual-policy machinery. The one real residual is that warmup measures eager while decode is served under graph, and the tuned winner **does** flip between eager and graph/host-excluded measurement at decode sizes (measured: `bmm_fp8` and `mm_fp4` flip at M≤64 on B200) — so a decode bucket measured eager can be suboptimal. The fix is not per-bucket or per-region policy (there is no scoped override — see above): it is that the single ambient policy should match the mode-sensitive path — `cuda_graph`, since decode is graph-served and is where the flips concentrate, while large-M prefill served eager is mode-insensitive (so measuring it under graph costs little). Per-bucket / per-region dual measurement policy is an explicit **non-goal**.

`cache_root` is placement only — schema and environment namespaces live below it, so no choice of root can mix incompatible entries (unlike the v1 filename, which is identity-bearing). Observability is the mitigation for ambient state: loud INFO at attach, once-per-op "source=managed cache" hit logs, and a planned `AutoTuner.explain()` provenance dump.

### Store layout and runtime behavior

```text
<root>/v2/
  <environment_hash>/
    manifest.json               # canonical environment, human-readable
    entries/<operation_hash>.json
```

`environment_hash` = SHA-256 of a canonical manifest (flashinfer / CUDA / cuBLAS / cuDNN backend + cudnn-frontend versions, GPU, cache schema, measurement policy). A version change produces a new directory; old directories remain (downgrade-safe). `operation_hash` hashes one autotune lookup key (op identity, bucketed dynamic dims, dtypes/layouts, runner extras) — repeated layers and different models share entries when keys are identical.

Runtime rules: lookup on in-memory miss reads one entry file; missing, malformed, or key-mismatched entries are **misses, never errors**; tuning publishes each winner immediately via tempfile + atomic rename (no exit-time save, no read/merge/write, no locks; concurrent writers do redundant work, last valid write wins). Hit/miss memoization lives inside the store object — never in v1 state — so the hot path never re-touches the filesystem and v1/v2 mixing is impossible by construction.

### MeasurementPolicy: tune the way you deploy

The primary axis is the **execution mode** — whether per-call host cost counts — not the timer implementation:

```python
MeasurementPolicy(execution_mode="auto" | "cuda_graph" | "eager", cold_l2=...)
```

| deployment | policy | what it measures |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA-graph serving | `execution_mode="cuda_graph"` | capture + replay timing; host cost excluded, as deployment does |
| eager serving | `execution_mode="eager"` | per-call host cost included: the eager sustained rate |
| default (`"auto"`) | today's behavior | delay-kernel timing; hides host cost within its budget |

Why one measurand cannot serve both (measured on SM100, `bmm_fp8`, decode-size M): the same cuDNN candidate reads **~8 µs** host-excluded but **~329 µs** as an eager sustained rate — its execute path costs ~155 µs/call on the host. Under an eager policy the backend ranking flips (cublas < cutlass ≪ cudnn), matching what eager frameworks actually experience. Even the fastest backends are host-bound at decode sizes (17–21 µs host vs ~8 µs kernel), so this is a regime property, not a one-backend anecdote. This is the same problem class raised in #3648/#3719; graph-mode profiling additionally requires capture-safe runners, so `"cuda_graph"` stays opt-in per the contract below until the runner suite is validated.

The policy is part of the store's environment identity: entries tuned under different policies select different winners and never overwrite each other.

**Aggregation on noisy hosts (added from SM120 field feedback).** Sub-0.05 ms kernels go bimodal under co-tenancy, and single-shot medians flip winners run-to-run — so "tune the way you deploy" only holds if the measurement is stable. Independently confirmed while building the accuracy harness (a shared engineering-sample board threw phantom winner-flips), the harness settled on **interleaved rounds** — every round measures all candidates back-to-back with a rotating start offset — which matches the interleaved min-of-medians the #3905 SM120 sweep converged on. A **policy-level repeat/aggregation knob** (rounds + reducer) is the right home for this so it applies to production tuning, not just the offline harness; proposed, not yet in #3861.

### Runner contract

A backend audit found the same disease in three forms: a tactic interpreted *relative to runner-internal shape-keyed state* (cuDNN plan indices into per-bucket plan lists; cuBLASLt algo-list indices re-enumerated at raw runtime shapes — including a silent wrong-algorithm replay and a silently-discarded-tuning bug; a device-dependent compile-cache key gap in CuteDSL). CuteDSL is otherwise the model architecture: caches keyed by the tactic itself, kernels take shapes as dynamic arguments — the tactic *selects* the cache entry instead of indexing into it.

The contract:

1. **Tactics must be self-describing** (explicit parameter tuples) or index a shape-independent static table — never an index into an object that varies with shape, library version, or enumeration order. (#3707's structured `(engine, knobs)` tactics bring cuDNN into compliance.)
2. **Runner-internal caches must be keyed by the tactic**, never by a runner-derived shape bucket; where a shape component is unavoidable, the resolved bucket is pushed down by the autotuner, not re-derived by convention.
3. **Compile/graph/algo cache keys must include device identity** and every trace-time-baked parameter.
4. **Revalidate at runtime** where cheap (the CUTLASS `isValidConfig` pattern): a stale tactic is a loud error or a clean fallback, never a silent different kernel and never a dead server (#3566's failure mode). Status: the autotuner-side hook (`validate_tactic(inputs, tactic)`, covering in-memory and on-disk hits) is in #3861; per-runner adoption — cuDNN first, via its #3707 structured tactics — is tracked separately, so #3566's class is *guardable*, not yet guarded, until runners implement it.
5. **`get_cache_key_extras` must be synthesis-invariant** (no raw dynamic dims) — violation is exactly the vllm#43119 failure class; a debug-mode completeness check should back this mechanically. This extends to any consumer-visible execution dimension a runner exposes: e.g. CuteDSL compile caches treat dynamic-vs-static batch as separate entries, so a warmup that exercises only one silently misses the other unless that dimension is in the key. (Measurement policy is already in the entry key, which closes the eager-warmup / graph-serving aliasing.)
6. **A serving-time miss must not trigger unbounded host-side compilation** (added from SM120 field feedback). Concrete failure: `bmm_fp8(backend="auto")` on an untuned serving shape falls onto the cuDNN runner, whose graph build is an `lru_cache` on the exact GEMM shape — reported as a 12–17 s host-side build *inside the engine loop* on sm_12x (vllm#48210). Measured on that exact hardware (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, cuDNN 9.24), a single plan builds in <1 s and a full `policy=ALL` enumeration is ~3 s, so the 12–17 s is per-shape *accumulation* (~325 ms/shape × dozens of distinct serving shapes). The common in-bucket case is already collapsed by cuDNN override-shape support (#2790 lineage — build once per bucket, execute real M via `override_shapes`); this contract rule is specifically the **out-of-bucket** residual — a serving shape outside every tuned bucket still cold-builds in the engine loop. Two candidate rules, either of which closes the class: the fallback (`tactic=-1`) path must be cheap, **or** runners declare an init-cost class so `auto` skips lazy-heavyweight backends outside a tuning context. This is a runner-contract addition (proposed, not in #3861); the default-candidate coverage guard only races `-1` *during* tuning and does not by itself bound serving-time compilation.

### Accuracy quantification

"v2 selects better tactics than v1" must be a measured claim. The harness: for a grid of (op, real-model N/K, M sweep), measure **every** valid candidate under deployment-faithful conditions at high repetition to obtain an oracle; then simulate tuner selections at production settings under each policy and score:

1. **Regret** — `(t(chosen) − t(oracle_best)) / t(oracle_best)` (headline metric; top-1 alone over-penalizes near-ties);
2. **Top-1 agreement** and rank correlation (noise vs bias diagnosis);
3. **Winner-flip rate** across repeated tuning runs;
4. **Replay fidelity** — does serving execute what the tuner chose (v1 has measured violations; the contract makes this structurally 100%);
5. **Bucket-transfer regret** — regret at off-representative M inside a bucket (decides round-up and bucket density with data).

The oracle sweep is expensive (hours of GPU for a few ops) and runs as a periodic quality gate, not per-PR. One methodological note from building it: candidates must be measured interleaved, not phase-separated, or thermal/clock drift between phases manufactures phantom regret; the sweep records the SM clock per round and clocks are deliberately **not** locked — deployments run floating clocks, and the lab should measure what the field runs.

**Validated on production silicon.** On a full-power B200 (183 GB / 1000 W, all-release stack) across `bmm_fp8` / `mm_fp4` / `cutlass_fused_moe`: on-diagonal regret (policy matches deployment) is ≈ 0, off-diagonal is catastrophic (>1000%), and v1's delay-kernel measurement is mediocre on both — the deployment-match thesis as a measured matrix. Two lessons the clock instrumentation earned: (1) an engineering-sample board threw **43–96% "MoE regret"** that was pure thermal artifact — the 64-expert GEMM collapsed its clock 1965→120 MHz mid-sweep, so `clk_ratio < ~0.9` must invalidate a row; (2) at *balanced* routing, MoE tactic selection is already ≈ 0% regret — which does **not** contradict #3622, because that regression is driven by *skewed* routing / effective per-expert M that a balanced probe cannot exercise. Representative-probe construction (the op-level track) is where that gap closes.

## Distributed story

Persistence and distributed orchestration remain separate responsibilities.

- **Shared filesystem: solved with zero framework code.** The per-entry atomic store makes all-ranks-tune-simultaneously (SGLang's default, and required whenever the dummy forward contains collectives) safe: concurrent publishes are redundant work and the last valid write wins. Per-rank cache files and framework hash directories become unnecessary. Precision on convergence: the *store* converges (and with it every later process/restart); ranks' in-session in-memory winners may still diverge until the finalize step below runs — `autotune_v2_reload()` (implemented in #3861): after a post-tuning barrier, every rank drops its locally-measured winners and re-reads the store's canonical entries, making all homogeneous ranks serve byte-identical tactics.
- **In-session rank consistency**: #3186 shows divergent per-rank tactic choices deadlocking NCCL symmetric-memory allocation *during* tuning. #3187 (all-reduce of measured times before argmin) fixes the in-session window; on top of the store we plan a **finalize step** (tune → barrier → reload winners from the shared store) guaranteeing byte-identical tactics afterwards, including across restarts. The two compose.
- **No shared filesystem** (multi-node, node-local roots): a small opaque boundary — `export()` produces bytes, the framework broadcasts them (never parses), `install()` verifies the environment fingerprint and publishes locally. Heterogeneous ranks must tune separately; a fingerprint mismatch refuses loudly. This is a distribution boundary, not a cache-management API; scheduling policy (leader-only vs all-ranks) stays with the framework.

## Roadmap

1. ~~Managed store + `autotune_v2()` opt-in~~ (**done** — #3861: store, env-hash isolation, atomic publish-on-tune, attach semantics, `MeasurementPolicy`, observability, GPU-free test suite covering both frameworks' consumption patterns)
2. ~~**Default-candidate coverage**~~ (**done** — in #3861: inside `autotune_v2` contexts the default path `(runners[0], -1)` always races as a candidate, so a tuned-and-persisted selection cannot lose to not tuning *at the probe inputs*. It is deliberately not claimed as a full regression guard: when the synthetic probe misrepresents serving — routing distribution / EP-sharded M, the #3622/#3537 class — the comparison itself is off; representative probe construction is op-level work on a separate track, and a paired default-vs-winner A/B with margin is a possible strengthening)
3. ~~**Rank-consistency finalize step**~~ (**done** — in #3861: `autotune_v2_reload()`, composing with #3187; see the distributed section)
4. **Opaque export/install** for multi-node distribution
5. **cuDNN plan sidecar** (after #3707): serialize the winning plan next to the entry, skip plan-list enumeration on load
6. **Framework migration**: vLLM and SGLang delete their hashing/broadcast/per-rank-file/knob code; deprecate the v1 path-based API afterwards (removal never deletes user files)

## Non-goals

Migration across incompatible environments; GC/size limits/pruning; a remote cache service; distributed locks or cross-job single-flight; **tuning of communication / multi-GPU collective ops** (v1 does not tune them either — collective tuning needs lockstep candidate enumeration, MAX-reduction, and one group-level decision, plus topology fields in the manifest; deferred until a concrete comm op wants tuning).

## Open questions

1. **Default execution mode**: `"auto"` currently preserves today's behavior. Flipping the default to `"cuda_graph"` (the dominant serving mode) requires the capture-safety contract validated across the op suite first. SGLang input (Brayden): decode is always CUDA-graph and prefill is moving there too, so eager-tuning accuracy is low-value for them — this strengthens the case for `"cuda_graph"` being the eventual default.
2. **Cold-L2 default**: currently off (inherits the op default). Field ask (Brayden) is cold-L2 **on by default**, since serving is cold more often than warm; the blocker is transient tuning memory (rotating buffers — already reduced to a single flush buffer on the CUPTI path). Candidate default-flip once the memory cost is bounded per op.
3. **Policy-level aggregation knob**: rounds + reducer (interleaved min-of-medians), so stable tactic ordering on co-tenant / noisy hosts is a production-tuning property, not just an offline-harness one (see MeasurementPolicy).
4. **Export/install surface**: exact spelling and whether a convenience `sync_across(process_group)` helper (following #3187's explicit-group precedent) is worth adding on top. Note (Brayden): SGLang intends single-rank-tune-then-broadcast for DP/TP — with a shared FS the store already gives this for free (one writer, all readers); export/install covers the no-shared-FS case.
5. **Bucket policy**: round-up vs round-down defaults, informed by bucket-transfer regret data rather than intuition (also raised in #3537's bucket-alignment discussion).
6. **Heuristic-competitive default** (Brayden): for well-behaved ops (e.g. CuteDSL NVFP4 GEMM) the un-tuned heuristic is already within noise, so autotuning's compile/tune cost buys little — the persistent store amortizes that one-time cost, and the accuracy harness's regret-of-`tactic=-1`-vs-oracle is exactly the metric to certify "safe to skip tuning here."

## Acknowledgments

This proposal incorporates feedback and examples from the vLLM team (opaque artifact boundary), Lee Nau (@leejnau) and the SGLang community (CUDA-graph lifecycle and capture safety), Brayden Zhong (@b8zhong) (#3648, #3719; cold-L2 default, single-rank broadcast, heuristic-competitive defaults, CUDA-graph-dominant deployment), @waynehacking8 (SM120 serving-time compilation bound, noisy-host aggregation, execution-mode cache keying), Po-Han Huang (@nvpohanh) and Albert Cheng (@qiching) (graph-profiling direction and capture-safe-runner requirements), Brian Ryu (@bkryu) (cold-L2 mismatch), Alex Yang (@aleozlx) and #3768 contributors (candidate quality and redundant compilation), and Yanqin Zhai (legacy-cache invalidation, #3707).

records.title: test(moe): cover do_finalize=False expert_weights dtype in the unified MoE fuzzer
records.body:
## Summary

The trtllm-gen routing kernel always emits expert weights in **bfloat16** (`routingData.mDtypeOutput` is hard-set to `Bfloat16` for every routing method in `csrc/trtllm_fused_moe_runner.cu`), independent of the `routing_logits` dtype. On the `do_finalize=False` path the `expert_weights` buffer is surfaced to the caller verbatim, so its dtype must be bf16 even when the routing logits are fp32 (the conventional DeepSeekV3 case). A mismatched fp32 label there reinterprets bf16 bytes as fp32 → garbage.

## Coverage gap

The routing-aware unified MoE fuzzer added in #3892 (`tests/moe/test_unified_moe_fuzz.py`) already parametrizes `routing_method × routing_input_mode × logits_dtype`, but it does not assert the dtype of the returned `expert_weights` on the `do_finalize=False` path. That specific combination (fp32 logits + `do_finalize=False`) is currently uncovered.

## Ask

Extend the unified MoE fuzzer (see #3892 for the relevant axes / oracle / dispatch code) so that, for each trtllm-gen fused-MoE operator:

- `trtllm_bf16_moe`
- `trtllm_fp8_per_tensor_scale_moe`
- `trtllm_fp8_block_scale_moe`
- `trtllm_mxint4_block_scale_moe`

run with fp32 (e.g. DeepSeekV3) routing logits and `do_finalize=False`, and assert the returned `expert_weights.dtype == torch.bfloat16` regardless of the `logits_dtype` axis.

This closes the fp32-logits + unfinalized path in the fuzzer and guards against future regressions of the routing-output dtype contract.

records.title: trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache: runFmhaReduction IMA on multi-bs CUDA graph capture (Gemma-4 hd=512, q_len=6)
records.body:
## Environment

- flashinfer-python / flashinfer-cubin **0.6.14**
- GPU: NVIDIA B200 (SM100)
- torch + CUDA 13
- Hit from SGLang Gemma-4-31B MTP verify CUDA-graph capture (`trtllm_mha`, `num_draft_tokens=6`)

## Summary

After [#3393](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/3393) / 0.6.14, the missing `headDim=512` KeepsMmaAb cubin for `q_len>=5` is fixed — a single decode call works.

But capturing **multiple** CUDA graphs over a hybrid stack (SWA `hd=256` + full `hd=512`, shared workspace) still blows up. With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` the failure is:

```
RuntimeError: Error in function 'runFmhaReduction' at fmhaReduction.cu:418:
Failed to launch kernel: an illegal memory access was encountered
```

Without launch blocking, SGLang often surfaces this later as `cudaErrorIllegalInstruction` on the next sync (rmsnorm / `.item()`).

Same script with `q_len=4` (Swaps path) passes.

## Geometry

Mirrors Gemma-4 global attn on TP=2:

| | full | SWA |
|--|--|--|
| head_dim | 512 | 256 |
| nQ / nKV | 16 / 2 (GQA=8) | 16 / 8 |
| window_left | -1 | 1023 |
| page_size | 64 | 64 |

`q_len_per_req=6` → `numHeadsQPerKv * q_len = 48` → KeepsMmaAb / tileSizeQ=64.

## Repro

Gist: https://gist.github.com/kpham-sgl/13efdff8b2d3e1c1aa40eb84501e1ab2

```bash
CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 python repro_fmha_reduction_cg.py
# fails while capturing bs=10 after 16/14/12 succeeded

CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 python repro_fmha_reduction_cg.py --q-len 4
# passes
```

Shared 512MB workspace, ~10 full + ~50 SWA calls per graph, capture bs `[16,14,12,10,...]` descending.

## What we ruled out / narrowed

- Not a missing cubin: raw `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` for `headDim=512`, `q_len∈{1,4,5,6,8,16}` works in eager.
- Isolated single-kernel CUDA graph for hd=512 / q_len=6 does **not** reproduce.
- Fresh / zeroed workspace and preallocated `out` do **not** fix it.
- Same-bs captured N times is OK; failure needs **several captures with different `bs`**.
- After the poison, later eager calls can also IMA in `runFmhaReduction`; a new process clears it.
- Sparse bs lists (e.g. `16 8 4 1`) have been OK in SGLang; the dense default list is what breaks.

## Expected

Multi-bs CUDA graph capture should work for this KeepsMmaAb geometry the same way `q_len=4` does.

## Related

- [#3343](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3343)
- [#3511](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3511)
- Fix [#3393](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/3393)

records.title: [RFC] Should FlashInfer explore an E0M3-based NVINT4 W4A4 path on Blackwell?
records.body:
## Status

This is an early-stage investigation, not a production-ready implementation proposal. The goal is to validate the observation, clarify its relationship to existing MxInt4 kernels, and determine whether a small community prototype is worthwhile.

## Proposal

I propose the working name **NVINT4** for a W4A4 format that reuses the NVFP4 scale hierarchy and block layout while replacing its E2M1 payload with E0M3:

- block size: 1 x 16;
- per-block scale: FP8 E4M3;
- tensor-level global scale;
- 4-bit payload:
  - NVFP4: E2M1, `±{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6}`;
  - proposed NVINT4: E0M3 sign-magnitude, `±{0, 1, ..., 7}`.

`NVINT4` is only a working name; it is not an official NVIDIA datatype.

## Blackwell observation

Black-box experiments on SM100 indicate that `tcgen05.mma.kind::mxf4nvf4` accepts an undocumented operand-format value that interprets the 4-bit payload as E0M3 instead of E2M1.

The A/B format fields appear independent, enabling:

- E0M3 × E0M3;
- E0M3 × E2M1;
- E2M1 × E0M3;
- E2M1 × E2M1.

Microbenchmarks observed the same instruction-level throughput for E0M3 and E2M1.

An independent SM120 experiment reproduced the E0M3 codebook through `mma.sync` SASS format bits and reported comparable E0M3/E2M1 throughput. A separate experiment also identified an E0M3 selector in Blackwell's `F2FP` conversion instruction.

Evidence and tooling:

- Initial SM100 observation: https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2059376150565089368
- SM120 reproducer: https://github.com/revollllt/sm120-e0m3-mma
- SM100 MMA/CVT tooling: https://gist.github.com/ShawRong/c29f327c2da690fd93e2b5e057cb76ad

These results demonstrate instruction-level behavior, not a supported ISA or an end-to-end inference speedup.

## Distinction from existing MxInt4

This proposal is not the same as the current TensorRT-LLM/FlashInfer MxInt4 path.

The existing public MxInt4 path uses:

- two's-complement signed INT4 `[-8, 7]`;
- block size 32 with BF16 scales;
- MxInt4 weights with BF16 activations;
- an MxInt4-to-BF16 MMA cast path.

Relevant sources:

- FlashInfer MxInt4 × BF16: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/2159
- FlashInfer launcher: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/trtllm_fused_moe_kernel_launcher.cu
- TensorRT-LLM GEMM datatype/cast validation: https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/main/cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/batchedGemm/trtllmGen_bmm_export/GemmOptions.h

Therefore, existing MxInt4 is primarily a W4A16 storage-and-cast path. The proposed NVINT4 would instead be a native E0M3 × E0M3 W4A4 path using Blackwell's FP4 MMA machinery.

## Why this may fit FlashInfer

FlashInfer already has NVFP4 quantization, scale layouts, dense GEMM and fused-MoE infrastructure. Related work includes the SM100/SM103 NVFP4 W4A4 RFC: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3380

If the observation is correct, an NVINT4 prototype may be able to reuse most of the NVFP4 infrastructure:

- packed 4-bit layouts;
- FP8 E4M3 block-scale layouts;
- TMA and scale interleaving;
- W4A4 GEMM pipelines;
- epilogues and framework-facing APIs.

The main differences would be the quantizer/codebook and the MMA operand format selector.


## Questions

1. NVINT4 could enable a native, full-throughput INT4-like W4A4 path on Blackwell. Is there meaningful community demand for such a path, and would it justify adding a new datatype and kernel stack? In particular, some workloads and studies have reported better quantization quality with uniform INT4-style codebooks than with FP4. ([INT v.s. FP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25602), [Adaptive Block-Scaled Data Types](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28765), [UFP4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20381))
2. If practical adoption depends on NVIDIA first exposing and supporting the required lower-level functionality—such as PTX, CUDA, or CUTLASS support—how difficult would it be for the open-source community to move this forward?
